title: Nothing outside

segments.voice: Yesterday, His play: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and bhaana mannana, accepting the will. Today, the one word that stanza keeps repeating.

You're stuck in traffic. Not moving. You're going to be late, and there's nothing you can do. The jaw sets, the fingers drum, and a voice in your head starts narrating how unfair this is, as if the traffic were happening outside the world, a glitch in how things are supposed to go. Most frustration has that shape: this shouldn't be happening. The first stanza of ashtpadi eleven has a single word it repeats, line after line, that answers the feeling. The word is hukam.
screen: `STUCK IN TRAFFIC.` → `THIS SHOULDN'T BE HAPPENING.` → `ONE WORD, LINE AFTER LINE.`

segments.voice: Hukam is the divine order, the command, the way God's will runs through everything. You met it last year in Japji. Yesterday's pictures, the earth held up with no support, things born and merging back, high and low, every color and form, all ride on one word, opening line after line: hukme, by the order. Guru Nanak said it plainly in Japji: everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside the hukam. Now the traffic jam. Frustration says: this is outside how things should be. Hukam says: there is no outside. The jam is inside the order. So is the meeting you'll be late for. So is your frustration. That doesn't make it pleasant. And it doesn't mean God personally put a truck in your lane to teach you a lesson; Sikh teachers don't usually read hukam as that kind of puzzle. It means the frustrating thing isn't a glitch in the universe. It's part of the same order that holds the earth up. When nothing is outside, there's nothing left to fight the way frustration wants to fight. Japji also says that whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I. The ego is the part that insists things go its way. Nothing outside quietly loosens it.
screen: `HUKAM: THE DIVINE ORDER.` · `HUKME, HUKME: BY THE ORDER.` · `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE THE HUKAM.` · `THE FRUSTRATION IS INSIDE TOO.` · then, large: `NOTHING OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring up something small that annoyed you today, a slow line, a rude message, a broken thing, and feel where it lives in you. Breathing in, say silently: this too is inside; breathing out: nothing outside; and let the feeling stay, held in the same order as everything else, until its edge softens even a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Nothing outside. Everything is within the hukam, the divine order, even what frustrates us; no one and nothing is outside it.
Your line: this too is inside. Even the traffic, even the frustration. Day four hundred eighty, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs understand hukam, the divine order, as encompassing everything, as Japji puts it, and many recall it in frustration or hardship as a way of loosening the ego's demand that things go its way.

fork.reveal: hukmai andar sabh ko: everything is inside the order, and that quietly loosens the ego's fight.

original.note: Gurmukhi: hukam, the divine order or command; 'hukme', by the order, drums through ashtpadi eleven's first stanza.

trapdoor: what you thought: hukam means God micromanages every traffic jam.
what it means: everything, even frustration, is inside one order; nothing is outside it.
what a scholar hears: hukam is an Arabic-Persian loanword (hukm, command) that Guru Nanak made central in Japji 2; understanding it is paired there with the end of haumai.
recall: lion, a name Sikh men carry
guess: all things, even frustrations, lie within God's order

chat.says: This traffic is ridiculous. Is there a Sikh idea for a moment like this?
options: Hukam: nothing is outside the divine order, not even this jam or our frustration.

chat.meaning: Japji says everyone is within the hukam and no one is outside it; the jam, the late meeting and the frustration are all inside the order.
